scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for a dad to force his 13-year-old son to play sports or join an extracurricular activity because the son is really lazy. The dad is frustrated because the son gets bad grades, doesn't take care of himself, and doesn't do anything unless he has to. The mom isn't helping, according to the dad, because she's enabling the behavior. The dad wants to snap the son out of this by making him join a team sport, thinking it will teach him work ethic and discipline. First, I need to understand the situation better. The son is 13, which is a tough age. He's in middle school, getting C's, which isn't great. He's disruptive in class, doesn't clean up after himself, and is very lazy. He only does things when forced, which is a problem because it's leading to poor habits. The dad is concerned that the son is heading towards a "loser" path, which is a strong term, but I can see the dad's frustration. The dad's plan is to force the son into a sport, like basketball, for a season. He thinks that being around peers who are working hard and having fun might give the son the push he needs. The dad is worried that if he doesn't do this, the son will continue with bad habits and lack a work ethic. Now, I need to think about whether forcing the son is the right approach. On one hand, the dad is trying to help the son develop better habits and a work ethic. On the other hand, forcing might lead to resentment or resistance. It's a tricky balance between pushing for improvement and respecting the child's autonomy. I should consider the potential outcomes. If the son is forced into sports, he might resist at first but could eventually see the benefits, like making friends, learning teamwork, and improving his physical health. It could also help him with time management and responsibility, which might translate into better grades and personal hygiene. However, forcing him might also backfire. The son could become more defiant, refuse to participate, or develop a negative view of sports and extracurricular activities. It might damage the relationship between the dad and the son if the son feels he's being controlled. Another angle is the role of the mom. The dad mentions that she's a terrible parent because she's enabling the son's behavior. That could complicate things because if the mom isn't on board with the dad's plan, it might lead to conflict or inconsistency in parenting, which isn't good for the child. I should also think about alternatives to forcing. Maybe the dad could have a conversation with the son about the importance of being active and having a work ethic. He could offer choices about which activity to join, giving the son some control. Positive reinforcement for small improvements might encourage better behavior without forcing. It's also important to consider the son's feelings. At 13, he's starting to seek independence and make his own choices. Forcing him into something might make him feel like he's not being heard or respected. It could affect his self-esteem and motivation. I wonder if there are other ways to instill a work ethic without forcing. Maybe assigning chores or responsibilities around the house could help. Or enrolling him in a class or activity he's interested in, which might naturally lead to more active participation. In terms of the dad's approach, he's considering making the son play basketball for a season, with the option to quit after that. That seems less harsh than making it a long-term commitment, but it's still forcing. The dad is hoping it will be a positive experience, but there's no guarantee. I also need to think about the dad's own feelings. He's frustrated and worried about his son's future. It's natural to want to help, but sometimes the methods we choose to help can have unintended consequences. The dad needs to balance his desire to help with the son's need for autonomy and respect. In conclusion, while the dad's intentions are good, forcing the son into sports might not be the best approach. It could lead to resistance and damage the relationship. Instead, the dad could try to involve the son in a way that gives him some control, uses positive reinforcement, and addresses the underlying issues like poor grades and hygiene.
